newsitem.title: INDIA: Rajiv Gandhi named in Bofors scandal - report.
newsitem.headline: Rajiv Gandhi named in Bofors scandal - report.

text.p: A week after entering the political arena, Rajiv Gandhi's widow on Wednesday faced a report in a leading newspaper naming her late husband as the prime accused in a big Indian corruption scandal.
The Indian Express said the Central Bureau of Investigation had sent a proposed chargesheet to the government for approval before filing charges through the courts.

The newspaper said the chargesheet named former prime minister Rajiv Gandhi as the main conspirator with several others in a kickback scam tied to a $1.3 billion artillery deal between India and the Swedish company Bofors AB 11 years ago.
Gandhi was assassinated in 1991 while campaigning.
The CBI was seeking clearance to prosecute former civil servants and others named in the chargesheet, the Express said.
Rajiv Gandhi all along denied any involvement in the 1986 guns deal, one of India's longest-running scandals. His family has also denied any involvement.
Reuters was unable to verify the report, carried exclusively by the Indian Express, a leading English language daily.
Italian-born Sonia Gandhi signed up last Thursday as an ordinary primary member of India's Congress, the party her husband's family dominated for decades.
The timing of her decision, after refusing for years to step into the political limelight following Rajiv's assassination, caught political analysts by surprise.
Most analysts cited the party's desperation to revive its fortunes by seeking to bring back the Gandhi political dynasty as the reason why the 50-year-old widow entered the political fray.
Congress is the second largest party in parliament after the main opposition Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).
Although it is in opposition, Congress provides vital support for the minority United Front coalition government led by Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral.
There has been intense speculation about what role Sonia Gandhi will play in coming elections to pick the party's president, a post currently held by 77-year-old Sitaram Kesri.
There had also been nagging questions whether the Bofors scandal would come back to haunt the Gandhi family.

The Indian Express on Sunday ran a cartoon depicting a missile, marked "Bofors Probe", looping lazily over the high walls of 10 Janpath -- Sonia Gandhi's Delhi residence -- while a Congress politician knelt in prayer outside the gates and a young boy warned him "Watch out. It could be a nuclear family."

Wednesday's Indian Express said the CBI report alleged that Rajiv Gandhi was guilty of conspiring to cause wilful loss to the state exchequer and of allowing middlemen to profit from the purchase of howitzers from Bofors.
The CBI report also said it had failed to prove that Gandhi had benefited financially from the deal, the newspaper said.
CBI officials were not immediately available for comment.
Swiss police say there is evidence that Bofors paid about $40 million into various bank accounts in Switzerland during the time the contract with India was drawn up and settled.
The CBI has previously already named Italian businessman Ottavio Quattrocchi and his wife, Maria, as recipients of illegal payments made by Bofors.
Quattrocchi was New Delhi representative of Italian engineering firm Snamprogetti Spa when India signed the deal with Bofors. He and Snamprogetti have denied any involvement in the alleged payments.
Quattrocchi now lives in Malaysia, and India has asked that country to arrest and extradite him and his wife.
The CBI has also named businessman Win Chadha, the Indian agent for Bofors, and his wife and son as recipients of the payments. Chadha, who lives in Dubai, denied the allegations.
